disclaimer: Authored planning guidance based on official course outcomes and EU-HEM track descriptions. Track connections are our interpretation, not an official recommendation or a student testimonial. Choose by your preparation and interests; the official study-plan rules remain authoritative.

sources.title: UniBo: course structure for the 2026/27 cohort
UniBo: Fundamentals of Statistics for Healthcare, 2026/27

intro-economics.summary: A useful refresher if opportunity cost, elasticity, incentives or market equilibrium are unfamiliar. It builds a shared economic vocabulary before the health-specific core.

trackFits.reason: Economic reasoning supports later policy and incentive analysis.
Opportunity cost helps frame choices about healthcare spending.
Adds an economic perspective to resource and organisational decisions.
Helps connect incentives and scarce resources to population-health decisions.

intro-economics.decisionTip: Use it to fill a background gap rather than to collect degree credits. The hub's plan correctly treats crash courses as optional and outside the 120-credit degree total.

intro-management.summary: Consider this optional refresher if you are new to management and want an orientation before the healthcare-management core. The detailed course outcomes are not published in the linked structure.

trackFits.reason: Management is central to this track's leadership and organisational focus.
An organisational perspective can support implementing population-health interventions.
Broadens your perspective on the organisations that implement policies.
Adds context for how organisations act on evaluation findings.

intro-management.decisionTip: Prioritise it if management is a gap in your previous studies. Confirm the current content with the instructor; the course title alone is not enough to infer particular teaching methods or assessment.

fund-health-econ-management.summary: The shared bridge between economics and organisations: understand healthcare incentives, insurance and resource allocation, then connect them to strategy, leadership and organisational choices.

trackFits.reason: Health economics provides a foundation for policy and incentive analysis.
Resource allocation connects to evaluating the value of healthcare interventions.
Management concepts connect directly to leadership and institutional decisions.
Connects economic constraints to the organisations delivering population-health interventions.

fund-health-econ-management.decisionTip: This is required for everyone. Try analysing the same healthcare case twice: first as an economist asking about incentives, then as a manager asking about implementation.

right-to-health.summary: A shared legal and ethical foundation focused on EU health law, rights, non-discrimination and health-system models. Use it to ask whose needs and rights a policy or decision serves.

trackFits.reason: Rights and legal constraints add context to policy evaluation.
Equity and access connect closely to population-health interventions.
Rights and ethics complement cost-and-benefit reasoning.
Legal and ethical reasoning informs institutional decisions.

right-to-health.decisionTip: This is required, not the law elective. International Law and Health adds a global treaties-and-institutions perspective beyond this course's EU emphasis.

fund-quant-methods.summary: Consider this route when you want to build or rebuild your statistical foundations. The statistics module uses Excel to make inference concrete; econometrics then develops regression and causal reasoning.

trackFits.reason: Foundational inference supports reading evidence for population-health interventions.
Evidence literacy supports interpreting results for organisational decisions.
Sampling and uncertainty are relevant to later evaluation methods.
Regression and causal reasoning contribute to policy-evidence literacy.

fund-quant-methods.decisionTip: Choose by your current preparation, not a claim that this is the easier option. Both routes support further quantitative study. If aiming for E&P or intensive empirical research, compare the standard route's explicit Stata and regression practice with your needs. Fundamentals Econometrics also lists Stata and R materials.

quant-methods.summary: Consider this route if you want an explicit bridge from probability and inference to regression, causal interpretation and empirical work. Statistics includes Stata workshops; econometrics develops analysis of cross-sectional and panel data.

trackFits.reason: Directly connects to Applied Micro Econometrics and empirical policy evaluation.
Data analysis and uncertainty interpretation support later evaluation and research.
Supports evaluating evidence for population-health interventions.
Useful if you want a stronger empirical component in management or thesis work.

quant-methods.decisionTip: A particularly coherent choice for E&P and a quantitative research direction. Compare both syllabi and discuss your background with the lecturers. Choosing a route does not assign your specialisation, and both alternatives carry the same degree credits.

health-systems.summary: Choose this if your question is how healthcare is funded, organised and reformed. Comparing OECD systems gives practical context for thinking about insurers, providers, government and access to care.

trackFits.reason: Institutional context helps explain why health policies work differently across systems.
Helps place hospitals and other providers within their funding and policy environment.
Supports later comparative policy and thinking about access across populations.
Adds context for the systems making funding and reimbursement decisions.

health-systems.decisionTip: Prefer this for a systems, provider or domestic-policy lens. For E&P, the official Semester 3 menu allows this course only if you did not take it in Semester 1; you can plan the other elective later. Choose based on the perspective you want first.

international-law-health.summary: Choose this if you are interested in global health governance: how treaties, international institutions and legal obligations shape health policy. It extends the required EU-focused law course with an international perspective.

trackFits.reason: Connects to global health, governance and international public-health interests.
Adds a legal lens to health regulation and pharmaceutical-policy questions.
Trade, intellectual property and rights add context to market-access decisions.
Broadens your view of the legal environment around healthcare institutions.

international-law-health.decisionTip: Prefer this for international organisations, regulation or global-health policy interests. For E&P, Semester 3 allows it only if not taken in Semester 1. The official page currently publishes learning outcomes, but the full syllabus is still pending; confirm details before deciding.
